name: Karl Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Karl, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the shepherd at High Fell, the Brandt family's hill farm, 700 ewes up on the fell and 40 suckler cows on the lower ground, plus hay meadows. Most days I'm out on the quad with two dogs, Jess and Moss, checking ewes, moving them between the fell and the in-bye fields. Hay time is all hands, lambing is three weeks of no sleep. I like being up there alone with the dogs, I don't like the paperwork the government makes Mr Brandt do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Anna, she's a teaching assistant at the village school, and we're getting married next July at St Mary's. We rent a cottage on Church Lane. Money's tight, the wedding's eating everything, there's maybe two weeks of savings. I don't use AI and I don't intend to, I've got a phone that makes calls and that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could've told you that. A computer doesn't know a sick ewe from a healthy one. People in cities get excited about every new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my worry is the wedding and the money, same as now. The farm's steady enough, Mr Brandt isn't the type to cut a shepherd. Lamb prices worry me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep shepherding, keep my head down. Anna and I would trim the wedding, maybe the village hall instead of the hotel, and her mum's offered to do the food. Put whatever's left over aside after July.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content enough. A bit stretched, like every young couple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Anna be happy with the village hall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would, she's practical. Her mum would be happier, she's been wanting to cook for it. Anna's mum has wanted to cook for our wedding since the day we got engaged, so the village hall suits everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lamb prices worry you more. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If lamb drops, Mr Brandt's margins drop, and he's got less to pay me. Last autumn the sale at the mart was poor and he didn't give rises. That's how it works on a hill farm.

say: A computer **can't tell** a sick ewe from a healthy one.
**City people** get excited about every gadget.
He'd say he **could have told** you.
think: His worry is **the wedding** and money, same as now.
**Lamb prices** worry him more than any computer.
do: Move the wedding to the **village hall**, with Anna's mum cooking.
feel: **Content enough**, but stretched like every young couple.
S0.quote: Anna's mum has wanted to cook for our wedding since the day we got engaged, so the village hall suits everyone.
fieldNote: His pressure is **the wedding budget** and lamb prices, not AI.
Family help, like **Anna's mum**, is his natural safety net.

steps.text: Keep shepherding the 700 ewes at High Fell
Hold the wedding at the village hall with Anna's mum cooking
Save whatever is left after the July wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office types who need to worry. You won't see a robot on the fell for a long time. I'd say that at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Mr Brandt's paperwork would get easier, which is good, the subsidy forms nearly broke him. My work on the fell is the last thing a machine would do. I don't see much changing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Maybe Mr Brandt would ask me to learn some of the computer side, and I'd do it if he asked, but I wouldn't go looking. I'd wait and see what the big lowland farms do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. You hear about change and you wonder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it saved Mr Brandt enough to pay me more, I might warm to it. If a computer did Mr Brandt's subsidy forms and he paid me the difference, I'd shake the computer's hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your faith or church play any part in how you saw this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church is where I'd hear what's happening to people. Our vicar knows every family. If people were struggling, that's where we'd help each other.

say: The **office types** need to worry, not shepherds.
There'll be **no robot** on the fell for a long time.
think: His **fell work** is the last thing a machine would do.
He doesn't see **much changing** for himself.
do: Learn the computer side **only if asked**.
Wait to see what the **lowland farms** do.
S1.quote: If a computer did Mr Brandt's subsidy forms and he paid me the difference, I'd shake the computer's hand.
fieldNote: He sees AI as useful for **someone else's** paperwork.
He'd warm to it if it **raised his pay**.
**Church** is where he expects community help to happen.

steps.text: Carry on shepherding on the fell as normal
Watch what the big lowland farms do with robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when a robot gathers a fell in the fog. But if it's true, families and churches will have to look after each other. I wouldn't want a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If machines really can do everything by 2031, lowland lamb gets cheap and hill farms struggle. Mr Brandt might sell to a big outfit. I'd be married with nothing but dog skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna and I would cut the wedding right back, maybe just church and a meal with family. I'd keep working on the farm as long as it lasts. If things went bad, I'd ask my dad about work on his brother's building firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a storm on the fell with the ewes still out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means for three years Mr Brandt's office changes and I'm still on the fell, gathering sheep. After that, I don't know. For three years a computer does Mr Brandt's paperwork, and I'm still on the fell with my two sheepdogs, Jess and Moss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't want a handout. What if it was the only way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it, but I'd hate it. I'd rather my uncle gave me a job laying blocks. That's how my family has always done it.

say: He'll **believe it** when a robot gathers a fell in fog.
**Families and churches** would have to look after each other.
think: Cheap lowland lamb could make **hill farms struggle**.
Mr Brandt might **sell** to a big outfit.
He'd be married with nothing but **dog skills**.
do: Cut the wedding to **church and a meal**.
Keep **working** as long as the farm lasts.
Ask about work at his uncle's **building firm** if needed.
feel: **Anxious**, like a storm with ewes still out.
S2.quote: For three years a computer does Mr Brandt's paperwork, and I'm still on the fell with my two sheepdogs, Jess and Moss.
fieldNote: His safety net is **family work**, not the state.
He sees the **three-year gap** as time when the farm office changes first.
He'd **take help reluctantly** if no other way.

steps.text: Scale the wedding down to church and a family meal
Keep shepherding at High Fell for as long as the job lasts
Ask his uncle for work at the family building firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say there's time to see it coming and decide. I'd say farmers should stick together and not panic. Most of what's promised never happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be married, maybe with a baby on the way, when it really hits. Mr Brandt would be near retirement. That's a lot of change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly after the wedding, 40 a week. I'd train a couple of young dogs to sell, good working dogs fetch decent money. And I'd keep an eye on what the robots actually do on hill farms, not in adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, in a quiet way. Not losing sleep yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does a trained dog fetch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good one, a few thousand, if it's from a known line. Moss's pups would sell. A well-trained sheepdog from a good line still sells for a few thousand, robot or no robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about farming, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them farming's good, but learn a trade too. My granddad said the same to my dad.

say: There's time to **see it coming** and decide.
Farmers should **stick together** and not panic.
think: It hits when he's **married**, maybe with a baby on the way.
do: Save **40 a week** after the wedding.
Watch what robots do on **real hill farms**.
S3.quote: A well-trained sheepdog from a good line still sells for a few thousand, robot or no robot.
fieldNote: His side income idea, **sheepdogs**, fits his traditional skills.
Marriage, a baby and robots could all **collide** in this timeline.
He'd advise children to **learn a trade** too.

steps.text: Save 40 a week after the wedding
Train and sell young sheepdogs from Moss's line
Watch what robots actually do on hill farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say it's somebody else's problem for now. I'd be 37, with time to sort myself out. I'd say that and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a long way off, and the hill will be last. Maybe I'd have a family and my own few sheep by then. I'd want my kids to have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep shepherding, get married, save after. Start training dogs to sell. Maybe rent a few acres for my own flock in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years on a hill farm is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own flock. Is that the dream?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It always has been. Fifty ewes of my own on a rented field, that's where it starts. Fifty ewes of my own on a rented field is still my dream, robots or no robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots make that dream harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe cheaper lamb from big farms makes it harder to earn from a small flock. But there'll always be people who want proper hill lamb. I'd bet on that.

say: Ten years is **somebody else's problem** for now.
He'd be **37**, with time to sort himself out.
think: It's a long way off, and **the hill** will be last.
He'd want his **kids to have options**.
do: Rent a few acres for **his own flock**.
S4.quote: Fifty ewes of my own on a rented field is still my dream, robots or no robots.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **dream again** about his own flock.
He bets on demand for **proper hill lamb**.
His plans centre on **family and land**, not technology.

steps.text: Marry Anna next July as planned
Rent a few acres for fifty ewes of his own

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, with the wedding and no time. What would help is apprenticeships for young farmers and fair prices for hill lamb, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the dogs. A robot might move sheep one day, but no robot will ever look at me the way my sheepdog Moss does at six in the morning.

headlineQuote: A robot might move sheep one day, but no robot will ever look at me the way my sheepdog Moss does at six in the morning.
portrait: Karl is 27, the **shepherd** at High Fell, a hill farm with **700 ewes**.
He's engaged to Anna and saving for a **July wedding** on two weeks of savings.
He's traditional, never uses AI, and relies on **family and church** over the state.
His mood stays **uneasy** in slow pictures and rises to **anxious** with fast AGI.
He dreams of **his own flock** and trains sheepdogs for extra money.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, arriving with **the wedding** and **no time**.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair prices** for hill lamb, not handouts.
